**"The Repo"**

A veteran repo specialist narrates his most challenging vehicle recovery yet — a pre-dawn operation requiring him to bypass a home security system he personally installed, evade a dog whose feeding schedule he knows by heart, and hotwire a sedan whose quirks he's memorized over 80,000 miles — all while maintaining ruthless professional detachment about the fact that the delinquent owner listed on his work order is himself. Told in a single breathless vignette of sprinting, rolling, and fumbling with slim jims in the dark, the comedy escalates as he deploys every trick in his twenty-year career against his own countermeasures, narrating each obstacle with the clipped bravado of a man who refuses to simply walk inside and grab his keys off the counter because that would mean admitting this is personal. The action peaks when his own motion-sensor floodlights catch him mid-hood-pop and he has to outrun the neighbor who's already dialing 911, his interior monologue still insisting — between gasps — that this is the cleanest, most by-the-book repo he's ever run.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *The Repo*

---

## Beat 1: The Work Order — A Name on the Clipboard

**Concrete Action:** The narrator, sitting in his repo truck in a strip-mall parking lot at 3:47 AM, reviews tonight's work order with practiced efficiency. He reads off the details — make, model, color, VIN, months delinquent, address — in the same clipped professional cadence he's used for thousands of jobs. Every detail is rendered with the authority of a man who has done this for twenty years. Only gradually, through accumulating recognitions the narrator refuses to mark as recognitions (a street name he knows, a sedan color he doesn't need to look up, a delinquent-owner name he declines to linger on), does the reader assemble what the narrator will not state: the debtor is him. He finishes his thermos of coffee, clips the order to his visor, pulls on his gloves, and puts the truck in drive.

**Narrative Technique: The Procedural Voice as Denial Infrastructure.** The beat opens *in medias res* — not of action, but of routine. The narrator speaks in the register of competence: jargon-laden, clipped, faintly boastful. This voice is the story's entire structural gambit. It functions the way Gogol's *skaz* narrator functions — as a personality through which reality is filtered and, crucially, distorted. But where Gogol's narrator is digressive and chatty, this narrator is the opposite: conspicuously *tight*, omitting what a normal person would say first. The technique is revelation-by-absence. The reader notices what the narrator refuses to notice. The name on the work order should be the first sentence; it is the last detail, and even then it's handled with the same flat affect as the VIN. This withholding performs the narrator's psychology more efficiently than any interior monologue could.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The beat teaches the reader *how to read the story*. Every subsequent scene will operate on the same double-register: what the professional voice reports and what the human situation actually is. The reader's pleasure — and unease — comes from occupying both levels simultaneously. The work order is also the story's deepest joke crystallized into an object: a piece of bureaucratic paper that transforms a man's relationship to his own life into a transaction. He could simply not do the job. He could call in sick. He could walk inside and grab his keys. That he instead clips the order to his visor and drives to his own address is the first clue that what looks like comedy is actually a man in crisis performing the only identity he has left.

---

## Beat 2: Casing the House — Reconnaissance of a Life

**Concrete Action:** The narrator pulls past the target address with headlights off and executes a standard drive-by assessment, narrating the property's tactical features: fence height, driveway grade, sightlines from neighboring houses, position of the vehicle. But each observation carries a second, unspoken layer. He notes the porch light is on a timer set to 11 PM — *because he set it*. He catalogs the fence's weak point by the side gate — *because he never got around to fixing it*. He registers that the garbage cans are at the curb a day early, which tells him something about the state of the occupant's routines, and a flicker of something (concern? recognition?) surfaces in the voice before being immediately suppressed by tactical analysis. He circles the block, parks three houses down, kills the engine, and begins his approach on foot.

**Narrative Technique: The Expert Gaze Turned on the Self — Dramatic Irony as Structural Engine.** This beat establishes the story's dominant mode of irony, which is not situational but *epistemic*. The narrator knows everything a repo man could know about this target — and vastly more. His professional observations are comically over-informed. He doesn't *estimate* fence height; he knows there are two missing slats because he was going to replace them in April. The technique requires the narrator to continually frame personal knowledge as professional intelligence, which produces a specific comic rhythm: clinical observation, followed by a micro-detail too intimate to be professional, followed by a swift return to jargon. Each cycle is a tiny failed repression. The reader begins to feel the structure beneath the comedy — a man narrating his own dispossession in the only language he still trusts.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The garbage cans. In a story built on refusal of sentiment, this single domestic detail — cans out on the wrong night, a disrupted routine — does more emotional work than any explicit confession could. The narrator processes it as intelligence ("occupant's schedule may be irregular, which introduces variables") when it obviously means something far bleaker. Gogol's method of burying feeling inside material objects — a coat, a toenail, a snuffbox — is replicated here: the story's emotional life will be carried entirely by things. Fence slats. Porch timers. Garbage cans. The narrator cannot speak about himself as a person, so the objects speak for him.

---

## Beat 3: The Security System — Defeating Your Own Defenses

**Concrete Action:** The narrator reaches the side door and confronts the home security panel — a system he personally selected, purchased, and installed. He narrates the approach as a professional challenge: "Sentinel-4 residential package, thirty-second entry window, keypad on the interior west wall." He pulls a bypass tool from his belt, then hesitates. He knows the code. His fingers know the code. But entering the code would mean *crossing the threshold of the house*, and the work order is for a vehicle recovery, not a residential entry. He stands in the dark having a procedural argument with himself about jurisdiction, scope of authorization, and professional ethics — a legalistic debate that is transparently a proxy for the emotional fact that he cannot bring himself to walk into his own home. He uses the bypass tool instead, defeating the system from outside with a workaround that takes four times as long, narrating the technical steps with evident professional satisfaction.

**Narrative Technique: The Procedural Detour as Psychological Revelation.** This is the story's first major escalation of its central absurdity: the narrator has the keys, knows the code, and could end the entire operation in thirty seconds by opening his own front door. His refusal to do so — justified through an elaborate scaffolding of professional protocol — is where the comedy and the anguish become structurally indistinguishable. The technique mirrors what Gogol does in the tailor scene: the *disproportion* between the available solution and the chosen path reveals the character's inner world more completely than direct access to his thoughts ever could. The narrator's interior monologue during the bypass is a masterclass in motivated reasoning, each justification slightly more strained than the last, building a comic rhythm of escalating self-deception that the reader can laugh at only because the alternative — feeling its full weight — is nearly unbearable.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The hesitation at the keypad. For one beat, the narrator's fingers hover over numbers he could press in his sleep, and the voice falters — not into emotion, but into silence. The gap in the narration, the half-second where the professional patter stops, is the equivalent of Akaky's "Leave me alone — why do you insult me?" It is the moment where the reader hears what the narrator *cannot say* beneath what he does say. Then the voice resumes, crisper than ever, and the reader understands: the bypass tool is not a tool for defeating a security system. It is a tool for not going home.

---

## Beat 4: The Dog — A Loyalty He Can't Repo

**Concrete Action:** Rounding the corner of the house toward the driveway, the narrator encounters the dog. He narrates the threat with professional gravity: "On-site canine, approximately sixty pounds, breed indeterminate, noted as hostile on the assessment." But the dog knows him. It approaches not with barking but with tail-wagging, sniffing, and the full-body wriggle of recognition. The narrator attempts to maintain protocol — he reaches for the dog treats every repo man carries — but the dog ignores the treats and pushes its head into his thigh, a gesture so specific and familiar that the narrator's voice briefly cracks into a different register: he says the dog's name. Just the name, once. Then he corrects course, notes the canine has been "neutralized," and steps around it toward the vehicle. The dog follows him. He tells it to stay. It stays — trained by him — and watches from the porch.

**Narrative Technique: The Sentimental Object That Refuses to Play Along.** Where the security system cooperated with the narrator's professional framing — it was, after all, a genuine obstacle to bypass — the dog breaks the performance. It introduces a category of response that the professional register cannot process: *love*. The narrator's entire operation depends on treating his own life as a target, but the dog has not received the work order. It simply recognizes him. Gogol uses this technique with the young clerk who hears "I am your brother" — inserting a witness whose unscripted reaction exposes the constructed nature of the surrounding performance. The dog functions as an involuntary truth-teller. Its body (the wriggle, the head-press) speaks a language the narrator's voice actively works to suppress, and the comic tension between the narrator's jargon ("canine neutralized") and the dog's evident joy is where the beat derives its power.

**What Makes It Memorable:** He says the dog's name. In a story built on the narrator's refusal to name what is happening, this single proper noun — uttered instinctively, before the professional voice can intercept it — is a structural detonation. It's a one-word breach in the façade, and the narrator patches it instantly, which makes the repair visible and therefore devastating. The detail of the dog *staying* on command — obedient to training the narrator provided — adds a final layer: even in the act of dispossessing himself, he is obeyed. The loyalty persists after every other claim on this life has been revoked. The dog watching from the porch as he works on the car becomes the story's silent emotional center.

---

## Beat 5: Hotwiring His Own Car — The Intimacy of Machinery

**Concrete Action:** The narrator reaches the sedan and begins the recovery. He pulls a slim jim from his kit to work the door lock — and fails. Then fails again. He knows why: there's a trick to this lock, a hitch in the mechanism he'd been meaning to fix, where you have to jiggle the tool at a specific angle while pulling the handle. He executes the trick automatically, from muscle memory, then catches himself and narrates the success as expert skill: "Experience with this model tells me the lock assembly has a common tolerance issue." Under the dash, hotwiring, his hands encounter the car's specific electrical personality — the fuse he'd replaced with the wrong amperage, the wire splice from when the stereo shorted on a road trip, jury-rigged fixes only he would know about. Each quirk is both the obstacle and the shortcut. He works with — and against — his own mechanical autobiography. The engine turns over on the second try. He knows about the second try. The car starts not because he's a skilled repo man but because he has turned this key (figuratively and literally) over 80,000 miles.

**Narrative Technique: Institutional Knowledge vs. Intimate Knowledge — The Comic Collapse of the Distinction.** This is the story's set piece, its equivalent of Gogol's saving-montage — the sequence where the central absurdity is pressurized until it becomes almost philosophical. Every repo man has generic vehicle knowledge; this narrator has *biographical* vehicle knowledge. The comedy escalates as the gap between the two kinds of knowing becomes impossible to maintain. The jury-rigged stereo wire is the key detail: it is a repair that could only be known to the owner, narrated as though it's a professional assessment. The reader watches the narrator knowingly deceive himself in real time, and the technique makes complicity unavoidable — we are *in his voice*, hearing his rationalizations from the inside, which means we are either laughing at his denial or sheltering inside it with him. Gogol's double-edged montage (the saving period that makes Akaky both more alive and more pathetic) finds its structural echo here: the longer the narrator works on *his own car with his own tools using his own knowledge while pretending it belongs to a stranger*, the more impressive and the more heartbreaking the performance becomes.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The road-trip stereo splice. In the middle of a technical procedure narrated with surgical detachment, the narrator's hands find a piece of wire that is, unmistakably, a memory — a specific day, a specific trip, a specific life in which things broke and got fixed imperfectly and kept working anyway, the way lives do. He doesn't narrate the memory. He narrates the wire gauge. But the reader constructs the memory anyway, because Gogol's rule applies: the object carries the feeling the voice refuses to. Eighty thousand miles is not a mileage figure. It is a compressed autobiography, and the narrator has just hotwired it.

---

## Beat 6: The Floodlights — Caught by Your Own Eyes

**Concrete Action:** The narrator pops the hood to disable the GPS tracker (which he installed, on a previous vehicle, for exactly this scenario — a detail he notes with grim professional approval). As he leans over the engine bay, the motion-sensor floodlights he mounted above the garage — positioned for exactly this angle, at exactly this sensitivity — blaze on. The entire driveway turns white. He freezes mid-reach, lit up like a stage performer. Across the street, the neighbor's bedroom light clicks on. The narrator can see the silhouette reaching for a phone. He knows this neighbor. He knows the neighbor is dialing 911 because *he told the neighbor* to call 911 if anyone was ever in his driveway at night. He slams the hood, throws himself into the driver's seat, and peels out — no longer narrating with clipped professionalism but with the breathless, adrenalized syntax of a man in genuine flight, even as the interior monologue continues to insist, between gasps, on the textbook legality and procedural beauty of what he is doing.

**Narrative Technique: The Catastrophic Convergence — All Self-Made Systems Firing at Once.** This is the story's climax, and its technique is architectural: every precaution the narrator built as a homeowner now activates against him as a repo man. The floodlights, the neighbor's vigilance, the security consciousness — all of it is *his own design*. The comedy reaches its apex because the trap is perfect and entirely self-constructed. Structurally, this mirrors Gogol's robbery on the dark square — the sudden stripping away of everything the narrative has built — but inverts it. Where Gogol goes spare and bare, this story goes loud and bright. The floodlights are the anti-darkness: instead of being robbed in anonymity, the narrator is exposed in total visibility, caught by his own surveillance state. The shift in the narrator's syntax — from controlled clauses to run-on, gasping fragments — is the formal announcement that the professional persona has finally cracked under kinetic pressure, even if the *content* of the monologue stubbornly refuses to acknowledge it.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The neighbor. Like Petrovich the tailor, like the young clerk who hears "I am your brother," the neighbor is a minor character who becomes the fulcrum of the scene's meaning. The narrator *told this man to make this call*. He built the system that is now treating him as an intruder in his own life, and the final, vertiginous joke is that *the system is working correctly*. He is, by every technical and legal definition available to the work order clipped to his visor, a man stealing a car from a delinquent debtor's driveway. narrative_story:
# The Repo

---

The work order comes off the printer at the yard same as any other. I pull it at 3:47 AM under the sodium lights of the Crossroads Plaza parking lot, engine idling, coffee still hot in the thermos. Twenty years of nights like this and you develop a rhythm. You don't rush the paperwork. You don't skip the details. Details are what separate the professional from the cowboy, and cowboys get shot.

I hold the sheet against the clipboard and read it down.

Vehicle: 2019 Honda Accord LX. Sedan. Four-door. Lunar Silver Metallic. I know the color without checking the code chart, but that's not unusual — you pull enough Accords, you learn the palette. VIN: 1HGCV1F14KA039___, the last three digits smudged by the printer but legible if you tilt the page. Lien holder: Pacific Range Credit Union, Glendale branch. Months delinquent: four. Four months is deep. Four months means certified letters have been sent and ignored. Means phone calls have gone to voicemail. Means someone has been sitting in a room watching the envelopes pile up on a counter and doing the math and the math has not come out and still they have not called, have not negotiated, have not surrendered the keys to the dealer. Four months is where I come in.

Recovery address: 414 Sycamore Glen Court.

I know the street. You work the east side long enough, you know every street. The houses on Sycamore Glen are mid-'90s construction, three-bedroom, two-bath, fourteen-hundred square feet, vinyl siding in four approved colors. HOA keeps the yards tight. Low fences. Attached two-car garages with the driveways on a six-degree grade — steep enough to make a flatbed tricky, gentle enough for a wheel-lift if you know your angles.

Debtor name: listed on the order in the same font as every other debtor name I've ever read, which is what it is, which is a name I note and move past because the name is not the job. The job is the vehicle. I've told every trainee I've ever had the same thing: *You are not in the business of people. You are in the business of collateral.* The debtor's name goes on the form. The form goes in the file. The file goes to the lien holder. You go home.

I screw the cap back on the thermos. Pull on my gloves — nitrile under leather, standard for a quiet lift. Clip the order to the visor where the dome light catches it. Check mirrors. Check the wheel-lift rig in the bed by feel: boom, crossbar, L-arms, straps, all seated. I've checked it three times already tonight but you check it again because the one time you don't is the time the crossbar pin is loose and you're dragging a sedan down the 134 shooting sparks like a Roman candle and explaining to your insurance company why the CHP impounded your rig.

I put the truck in drive.

The route takes eleven minutes at this hour. No traffic. No reason to hurry and no reason to delay. The radio's off. Has been off for weeks, actually — the knob broke and I haven't replaced it. The silence is fine. I prefer to run the approach in my head before I arrive. Visualize the site. Anticipate the variables. Dog, no dog. Garage, driveway. Slope, flat. Neighbor proximity and sightlines. Time of night, day of week, phase of the moon if you want to get poetic about it, which I don't.

I turn onto Sycamore Glen with my headlights off at 4:02.

---

Standard approach is a two-pass reconnaissance. First pass, you drive the full block at fifteen miles per hour, windows down, taking inventory. You are a census taker of risk. Second pass, you confirm the vehicle's position and choose your angle.

First pass.

414 is mid-block, south side. I note the porch light is on — a yellow CFL behind a frosted sconce, set on a timer that trips at eleven and runs till dawn. A reasonable security choice. The kind of choice a man makes after reading the crime blotter one too many times, after deciding that a thirty-dollar timer from Home Depot is cheaper than the anxiety of a dark porch. I can see from the street that the bulb is the original — hasn't been changed in at least two years based on the color temperature, which has shifted toward amber the way CFLs do at end-of-life. A fresh bulb would be brighter. This one is tired.

The fence is cedar, four feet, running the property line to the back corner. Standard residential grade, nothing that would slow a professional down. There's a weak point at the side gate where two slats have pulled away from the rail — the bottom rail, where moisture gets in and the nails corrode. April project. The kind of thing you buy the lumber for on a Saturday, lean it against the garage wall, and then it's July and the lumber's still leaning and the slats are still loose and you've stopped seeing them because you walk past them every day and the eye stops registering what the hand hasn't fixed.

Vehicle is in the driveway, not the garage. That's favorable. A garage recovery adds fifteen minutes and a significant noise profile — you're dealing with door mechanisms, confined maneuvering, the amplified echo of every tool you drop. Driveway means open air, clean angles, faster egress. The Accord is parked nose-in, which means I'll back the rig up to the rear axle and lift from behind. Standard.

I note the garbage cans. They're at the curb. Tomorrow — today, technically — is Thursday. Collection on Sycamore Glen is Friday. The cans are out a day early. Could indicate an irregular schedule. Could mean the occupant has lost track of the days, which happens — shift work, insomnia, the particular fog that descends on a person when the mail is all past-due notices and the phone is all unknown numbers. Could mean nothing. I note it as a variable and move on.

Second pass. Vehicle confirmed: silver Accord, rear plate visible, first three characters match the order. Driveway grade is manageable. No vehicles on the street within three houses in either direction. Porch light, as noted. Front windows dark. No indication the occupant is awake.

I park three houses east, on the north side, tucked against the curb beneath a jacaranda that hasn't been trimmed in a season and hangs low enough to break the silhouette of the truck cab from the street. Kill the engine. Sit for sixty seconds — standard cooling period, lets the neighborhood settle around the sound of your arrival. A dog barks two blocks over, then stops. Somewhere a sprinkler system clicks on and begins its arc.

I take the slim jim, the bypass kit, and the under-dash tool roll. Close the door with my hip, no slam. Begin the approach on foot, staying on the grass margin where my boots don't report against concrete.

The houses on this side of the street are all dark except for the usual constellations of standby lights — router LEDs, microwave clocks, the blue pulse of a smoke detector low on battery. Normal. A neighborhood at rest. I cross the street at an angle that keeps me out of the direct cone of 414's porch light and come up along the fence line on the east side, where the shadows are deepest.

The loose slats are right where they've always been.

---

The side door is the preferred entry vector for the yard — it opens to the narrow run between the house and the fence, gives direct access to the driveway without crossing the front of the property. The door is a thirty-two-inch steel-core, solid but nothing special, secured by a Kwikset single-cylinder that any repo man with a tension wrench could defeat in under a minute.

But the door also puts me within arm's reach of the security panel.

Sentinel-4 residential package. Thirty-second entry window. Keypad on the interior west wall, left of the door frame, mounted at fifty-four inches — chest height, so you can punch the code in the dark while holding groceries, which was the idea, which was the logic when the system was selected from a catalog and comparison-shopped across three brands and installed over a weekend with a drill, a fish tape, and a level that kept rolling off the stepladder.

The panel will be armed. A man four months behind on his car payments might let a lot of things slide, but the security system is a monthly charge buried in the credit card autopay, which means it's the kind of expense that persists even after conscious financial decision-making has collapsed — the zombie charge, we call it in the industry, the subscription that outlives the subscriber's solvency. The system will be armed and the thirty-second window will start the moment the side door opens, and if the code isn't entered, the monitoring company dispatches, and dispatch means sirens, and sirens mean a blown job.

Now. Technically. I could enter the code.

I could open this door, step inside, cross the three feet of linoleum between the threshold and the panel, and key in the four digits that would silence the system before it ever spoke. It would take six seconds. I have done it — a person could have done it, in the general case — thousands of times. The fingers know. The fingers could do it in the dark, have done it in the dark, coming home at 4 AM from jobs exactly like this one, the hand reaching for the panel before the eyes adjust, the beep-beep-beep-beep of the code entered by pure proprioception, the chime of acceptance, then the silence of a disarmed house.

But that would constitute residential entry. The work order authorizes vehicle recovery from the listed address. It does not authorize entry into the dwelling. Section 9-503 of the Uniform Commercial Code permits the secured party to take possession of collateral without judicial process provided it proceeds without breach of the peace. *Without breach of the peace.* Entering a residence — even an unlocked residence, even a residence whose code you happen to know through, say, professional experience with Sentinel-4 systems, which use a common factory default that many owners never bother to change — entering a residence crosses the line from repossession to trespass, and trespass is a breach of the peace, and a breach of the peace voids the self-help remedy, and a voided self-help remedy means the lien holder has to go to court, which means lawyers, which means delay, which means I don't get paid and the job goes back in the queue and someone else pulls it next week and probably botches it because they don't — because they won't have the site-specific intelligence I've developed during this reconnaissance.

So. The bypass tool.

I pull the RF jammer from the kit — a device about the size of a deck of cards that floods the Sentinel-4's wireless frequency with noise, effectively deafening the panel to its own sensors. It won't stop the countdown if the door is opened, but it will prevent the door sensor from reporting to the panel in the first place. The trick is positioning: you need to get the jammer within eighteen inches of the door-frame magnet, which means mounting it on the exterior wall and hoping the signal penetrates the siding.

On vinyl-sided houses with standard insulation, penetration is inconsistent. Wood frame helps. Foil-backed insulation kills it. I don't know what insulation — I would have to guess, based on construction era and regional building codes, what insulation is behind this particular wall, and the truth is that mid-'90s tract homes in this area used R-13 fiberglass batts, no foil backing, which gives me roughly a seventy percent success rate with the jammer.

I could just enter the code.

I position the jammer against the siding with a strip of mounting putty, one inch left of the door-frame magnet, and hold my breath. Open the door. The linoleum inside is — the linoleum is standard residential grade, a pattern I don't need to describe. The panel is right there, green LED steady, the display showing ARMED in sans-serif capitals, and the thirty-second window does not begin, which means the jammer is working, which means the door sensor is blind, which means I have bypassed a Sentinel-4 residential package from the exterior without breaching the dwelling.

Four times as long as entering the code. But clean. Professional. Within scope.

I retrieve the jammer, close the door, and proceed along the side of the house toward the driveway.

---

The dog comes around the corner of the garage at a trot.

I see it before it sees me — or more accurately, it smells me before I see it, because it's already moving in my direction with its nose low and its tail at half-mast, the posture of a dog that has detected something interesting but hasn't yet classified it as threat or friend. Approximately sixty pounds. Breed indeterminate — some kind of Lab mix, maybe shepherd in the jaw, the kind of dog that the shelter lists as "retriever blend" because it moves adoptions. Noted on the assessment as potentially hostile, which is standard language for any on-site canine. You never assume friendly. You carry treats — liver-flavored, individually wrapped, effective on roughly eighty percent of residential dogs — and you carry pepper spray for the other twenty percent, and you make the determination in the first five seconds based on ear position, hackle state, and vocalization.

This dog is not vocalizing.

Its ears are forward but soft. No hackle. The tail has moved from half-mast to full sweep, a metronome of increasing enthusiasm, and it is closing the distance between us not in the stiff-legged, squared-off approach of a territorial animal but in the loose, slightly sideways amble of a dog that has just realized something wonderful is happening and cannot believe its luck.

I reach for the treats.

The dog ignores my hand entirely. It pushes past the offered treat and drives its head into my thigh — not a nudge, not a bump, but the sustained, full-weight lean of a dog that is trying to press itself into a person, the head buried against the leg, the body curving inward, the tail now moving so fast it's pulling the hindquarters with it in that full-body sine wave that dogs do when the tail alone is insufficient to express the magnitude of the situation.

This is not standard canine behavior toward a stranger.

I should note that some dogs are simply — some breeds are indiscriminate in their —

"Benny."

The word is out before the professional voice can intercept it. One word, two syllables, spoken in a register I haven't used on this job. A name voice. The voice you use at the back door at 6 PM when the kibble hits the bowl and the nails come skittering across the kitchen floor. The dog — the canine — responds to the vocalization with intensified contact behavior, pressing harder, and I can feel through the leather glove the vibration of a whine so high-pitched it's almost inaudible, a sound produced in the very back of the throat, the sound a dog makes when a person it has been waiting for has finally, finally come home.

Canine neutralized. No pepper spray required. I step around the animal and proceed toward the vehicle.

The dog follows.

"Stay."

It stays. I don't have to look back. I know it stays because I can hear the absence of nails on concrete, and because I spent four Saturdays in a PetSmart parking lot with a clicker and a bag of chicken bits teaching it that exact command, and it was a good student, better than most — better than most dogs, is what I mean — and it learned to stay with a reliability that the trainer called exceptional.

I can feel it watching me from the porch. I don't look back. The job is the vehicle. The vehicle is thirty feet ahead of me in the driveway, and that is where my attention is directed, because I am in the business of collateral and the collateral is a 2019 Honda Accord LX and I am going to recover it now.

---

The slim jim slides between the window glass and the weather stripping with the practiced ease of ten thousand door locks in twenty years. You develop a feel. The tool's hook finds the linkage rod inside the door panel, and you apply lateral pressure — gentle, not forced, the way you'd work a lever you had some respect for — and the lock pops.

Except it doesn't.

I reposition. Try again. The hook is catching on something — a clip, maybe, or a secondary rod — and I can feel the geometry of the lock assembly through the tool the way a surgeon reportedly feels anatomy through a probe, and I know what the problem is. I know because this particular lock has a tolerance issue in the actuator housing where the linkage rod sits about two millimeters deeper than the Honda service manual specifies, a variance that is technically within factory spec but that, in practice, means the slim jim's hook slides right past the engagement point unless you angle the tool at roughly fifteen degrees off vertical while simultaneously — here — pulling the exterior handle to shift the rod into a reachable position.

The lock
